Layouts.line: The container of layout modules, walks each layout's coordinates to build the physical light set the mapping consumes.

Effects.line: The container of layers, composites them (blend mode + opacity per layer) into the final light buffer.

Layer.line: One rendering layer, an effect writes into its buffer, modifiers transform the coordinate mapping, and the layer composites onto the shared output.
Layer.summary: The unit the render loop iterates.

guide.title: Layer, details
guide.text:
**The buffer persists between frames**

Nothing clears the buffer per frame, which is the FastLED and WLED convention and the reason trails work at all. An effect can fade what is already there for a tail, or read prior pixels for a scroll or a Game of Life. Each effect owns its background: a full-grid effect overwrites every pixel, a trail effect fades and paints, and a sparse effect that wants a clean frame fills it first. The cold-path rebuild clears once, so a freshly added effect starts black.

**A fade is a rate**

An effect asks for a fade per reference frame of a sixtieth of a second, and the layer scales it by the fraction of that frame the real frame covered. A trail is then the same length on a 470 fps device and a 140,000 fps desktop. The layer keeps the gentlest request across every fading effect. Several fading effects then cost one buffer pass, and none fades another's fresh pixels.

**Compositing is the container's job**

`blendMode` and `opacity` live on the layer but the layer never reads them: it cannot know its own position in the stack or what sits beneath it. The `Drivers` container reads both values plus the child order and does the compositing, bottom layer first. Keeping the values here means they travel with the layer through add, delete and reorder, instead of a separate list that drifts out of sync.

**Two build paths**

The cold path folds the physical box through each enabled static modifier to get the logical box. It then builds the mapping with a counting-sort CSR: one pass counts destinations per cell, a prefix sum turns counts into offsets, and a second pass scatters. A dense grid in natural order with no modifier skips the table and takes an identity mapping, the frame-rate floor for the common case.

**What the status line reports**

The status shows the logical box the effects render into, which can differ from the physical box on `Layouts`: a mirror modifier folds a 128 by 128 physical layout into a 64 by 64 logical one. The same slot carries a warning when a build cannot fit in memory, and a warning always wins over the neutral box line.

Layer.alt: Layer container with a child effect

blendMode.line: How this layer combines with the ones below; a multiply layer is a mask over them.

Drivers.line: The container of driver modules, owning the shared buffer and the per-light output correction every driver applies before sending.
Drivers.summary:
Off scales the output to black while preserving `brightness`, so switching on restores the level. Every consumer drives it: the UI, infrared, the WLED app, Home Assistant and MQTT.

🎚️ `relayPins`: GPIOs switching the LED power supply, closed while `on` and brightness > 0.

On by default, and it falls back to single-core by itself when the extra frame buffer will not fit. The switch exists to compare the two.

Near zero means render and output overlap well, and a large value means core 0 idles on a slow output stage. Shown only while `multicore` is on.
Drivers.alt: Drivers container with the on/off + brightness controls

brightness.line: Global output brightness, multiplied with each driver's `localBrightness`.

palette.line: What effects sample from, built in or [scripted](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/light/moonlive.html); settable by name too.

multicore.line: Run the output stage on the second core.

renderWait.line: Read-only: how long core 0 waited for core 1 at the frame boundary.

FixtureProfilesModule.line: The named channel wirings drivers reference, which channel carries Red, Green, Blue, White, or a fixture role like Pan/Tilt.
FixtureProfilesModule.summary:
Real fixtures ship read-only (the color orders, multi-channel pars, moving heads); add your own alongside them. A driver stores the profile's name, so reordering never breaks a reference; after a rename, a driver on the old name falls back to its default at the next boot, as [Drivers](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/light/drivers.html) describes.

A row carries a name, a channel count, and one role picker per channel. Built-in rows are read-only, and custom rows persist across a reboot.

guide.title: FixtureProfiles, details
guide.text:
**16-bit channels**

A fine role is the low byte of a 16-bit channel, the DMX convention: `R fine`, `G fine`, `B fine`, `W fine`, `WW fine`, `Pan fine`, `Tilt fine` and `Dimmer fine`.
`RGB 16-bit`, `GRB 16-bit` and `RGBW 16-bit` ship built in, and a custom row places fine roles in any order a fixture needs.

The effects stay 8-bit, and the brightness and curve go to 16 bits on the way out, so a fade keeps all 256 steps at any brightness.
That takes a 512-byte table per driver; when it cannot be allocated the channel stays 8-bit, with a fine byte of 0.
Pan and tilt widen by repeating their byte, so a full 8-bit aim reaches the fixture's full 16-bit range.
A master dimmer is held wide open on both bytes.

**Which profile a chip takes**

A WS2811 orders its colors as the strip or puck maker wired it, so try `RGB`, then the other five orders.
The TM1814 and TM1914 send a settings preamble on an inverted line before the pixels, which a profile cannot describe.

profiles.line: The editable list of profile definitions, one row per profile.

CarLightsLayout.line: A pair of car headlights: concentric rings of lights placed like a car's front lamps.
CarLightsLayout.summary: Nested rings of 1, 8, 12, 16 and 24 lights form each lamp, with a ring of 32 more on the outer two. Side strips join them, in a fixed arrangement drawn with [Ring](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/light/layouts.html#ring) geometry.

scale.line: The overall size: the spacing out from each lamp's center.

CubeLayout.line: A solid 3D cube of lights, wired through the volume in the axis order you choose.
CubeLayout.summary: Every point of a `width` × `height` × `depth` box holds a light. The strip's path is yours to set: which axis it runs along first, which way each axis counts, and which axes snake back and forth. It is the 3D form of [Panel](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/light/layouts.html#panel).

wiringOrder.line: The axis order the strip follows, fastest first.

X++.line: Whether x counts up rather than down.

snakeX.line: Whether x snakes, reversing on alternate passes.

HumanSizedCubeLayout.line: A walk-in cube of five LED curtains: front, back, top, left and right, open at the bottom.
HumanSizedCubeLayout.summary: Each face is a curtain the size of the box's side, for a room-scale cube a person stands inside.

MoonLiveLayout.line: Where the lights physically are, written as text on the running device.
MoonLiveLayout.summary: A layout is the one part of the pipeline that differs for every build: a ring, a spiral staircase, a costume sewn last night. A script means the person who hung the lights describes where they went, and sees it at once. Everything the script declares appears as a real control. The language is [MoonLive](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/light/moonlive.html).

guide.title: How the light count is known
guide.text:
A layout answers how many lights before it produces a single coordinate, because the Layer sizes its buffer from that number and only then asks where each light is. A script cannot be asked how many without running it.

So it runs twice. The first pass counts what `addLight` places, and the second emits each position. Same script and same arithmetic, so a deterministic script agrees with itself, which is what the compiled layouts do for the same reason.

Nothing is stored between the passes. Staging 16,384 coordinates costs 48 KB, which a classic ESP32 driving that many lights does not have spare. Running the script again is cheaper than remembering what it said.

A script calling `random16` breaks that determinism. The passes disagree on the count when a random value decides a loop bound. A random coordinate keeps the count right, and places the lights elsewhere on the second pass.

guide.title: What a layout script is given
guide.text:
`addLight(x, y, z)` places the next light along the strand. There is no index, because the order the script calls it in is the strand order.

`t` is the one system variable a layout reads, and it is always 0: the script runs twice per rebuild and must agree with itself. `width`, `height` and `depth` read 0, since a layout is upstream of the grid it defines.

A script names its own size controls, such as `cols` and `rows`. The pipeline derives the bounding box from the coordinates placed, so a size passed in from outside would be a second answer that could disagree with the first.

script.line: Which `.mll` script runs, picked from the library and edited here.

PanelsLayout.line: An M × N grid of matrix panels, tiled into one large display for a video wall.
PanelsLayout.summary: The wiring is two walks, each set on its own: an outer one over the panel grid and an inner one over each panel's lights, as [Panel](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/light/layouts.html#panel) wires one.

wiringOrderP.line: Which axis the panel grid walks first.

X++P.line: Whether the panel grid's x counts up.

snakeP.line: Serpentine across the panel grid: alternate panel rows run in reverse.

wiringOrder.line: Which axis a panel walks first.

X++.line: Whether a panel's x counts up.

snake.line: Serpentine inside each panel: alternate lines run in reverse.

TorontoBarGourdsLayout.line: A bar's installation of 24 decorative gourds, each lit at one of three granularities: one light per gourd, per side, or per LED.

granularity.line: How finely each gourd is lit.
granularity.more: One gourd one light stacks a gourd's lights on its own position. One side one light gives each of a gourd's five sides one point, and one LED one light places every LED on its side's ring of 12. Both hold 61 lights a gourd, the middle one included.

nrOfLightsPerGourd.line: Lights per gourd when one gourd is one light.

GridLayout.line: A dense grid of lights in 1D, 2D or 3D: every position holds a light, wired row by row.
GridLayout.summary: The wiring runs x fastest, then y, then z, and a strip that snakes back and forth runs every other row in reverse.

depth.line: Its extent on z, 1 for a flat panel.

serpentine.line: Every other row runs in reverse, for a snaked strip.

GridBlacksLayout.line: A grid with dark columns held black in every row, for a sealed panel that must stay dark down a strip, or a slat wall.
GridBlacksLayout.summary: A dark column is still a wire position the driver clocks, so data flows through the unlit lights to the lit columns beyond. The lit columns keep their true positions, so an effect maps straight across the gap. Without dark columns it is a [Grid](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/light/layouts.html#grid).

serpentine.line: Every other row runs in reverse, matching a snaked strip.

blackCount.line: How many dark columns; none renders exactly like a Grid.

PanelLayout.line: A 2D matrix panel with full wiring control: the axis order, the direction per axis, and serpentine.
PanelLayout.summary: The general matrix layout, of which [Grid](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/light/layouts.html#grid) is the simple case.

X++.line: Whether x counts up rather than down.

snake.line: Serpentine wiring: alternate lines run in reverse.

RingLayout.line: A ring of lights evenly spaced around a circle, or an arc of one.
RingLayout.summary: The lights start at `angleFirst` and span `rotation` degrees, a full turn drawing the whole circle. A center of its own places the ring anywhere, which is how CarLights and Rings241 build their lamps and discs from rings.

nrOfLEDs.line: How many lights go around the ring.

angleFirst.line: The angle the first light sits at, in degrees.

rotation.line: The arc spanned in degrees, less than a full turn a partial ring.

scale.line: The spacing out from the center.

centerX.line: The center's x before scaling; 0 places the ring by its size.

centerY.line: The center's y before scaling; 0 places the ring by its size.

Rings241Layout.line: The classic 241-light disc: nine concentric rings of 1, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48 and 60 lights sharing a center.

scale.line: The size: scales the ring radii and the shared center.

outside in.line: Light 0 on the outer ring, wired inward rather than outward.
outside in.more: A disc is soldered either from the center light outward, the default, or from the outer 60-light ring inward, and this names which end of the wire is light 0. Only the ring order flips; each ring keeps the direction it is wired in.

angleFirst.line: The angle light 0 of each ring sits at, in degrees.

SingleColumnLayout.line: A vertical line of lights at a fixed x, the 1D column.

starting Y.line: The row the column starts at.

height.line: How many lights the column holds.

reversed order.line: Wire it top to bottom rather than bottom to top.

SingleRowLayout.line: A horizontal line of lights at a fixed y: the 1D row, a bare strip laid straight.

starting X.line: The column the row starts at.

width.line: How many lights the row holds.

reversed order.line: Wire it right to left rather than left to right.

SphereLayout.line: Lights on the surface of a hollow sphere: a shell one light thick, nothing inside.

SpiralLayout.line: A conical spiral: lights winding up a cone from a wide base to a point.

ledCount.line: How many lights wind up the spiral.

bottomRadius.line: The radius at the base, in light-units.

height.line: The vertical rise from base to tip.

TubesLayout.line: Parallel vertical tubes, each a column of lights, standing side by side.

nrOfTubes.line: How many tubes stand side by side.

ledsPerTube.line: How many lights each tube carries.

tubeDistance.line: The spacing between tubes, in light-units.

reversed.line: Wire each tube from its top.

WheelLayout.line: A bicycle wheel: spokes radiating from a center hub, each a straight row of lights.

spokes.line: How many spokes radiate from the hub.

ledsPerSpoke.line: How many lights each spoke carries.

AudioSpectrumEffect.line: The 16 mic frequency bands spread across X, each column lit bottom-up by its magnitude.
AudioSpectrumEffect.attribution: MoonLight original, on the WLED-SR GEQ / spectrum concept (Andrew Tuline) · via [MoonLight](https://github.com/ewowi/MoonLight/blob/main/src/MoonLight/Nodes/Effects/E_WLED.h)

colorMode.line: Bars colored by `height`, the VU look, or `per-band`, a rainbow.

RadialSpectrumEffect.summary: Each band owns a sector around the center, mirrored left and right with the bass at top and bottom. Sound is born at the center and travels outward, so the radius is time and a ring's length is that band's recent history. Every sector is one band, so a band that is stuck shows as a sector that never moves. On a cube the ripples are expanding shells.
RadialSpectrumEffect.attribution: MoonLight original, the radial spectrogram on `PolarLut` and the onset detector

speed.line: How fast sound travels outward.

persistence.line: How far out a ripple stays visible.

smooth.line: Read the meter ballistic rather than the raw bands.

beat.line: A white shockwave born at the center on every onset.

VuMetersEffect.line: Sixteen needles, one per band, each with real mass.
VuMetersEffect.summary:
What makes a VU meter beautiful is not the dial, it is the needle: it overshoots a peak, swings back and settles, which is why a mechanical meter reads as alive where a bar graph reads as a readout.

The bass needles are heavier than the treble ones, so the low end swings and the high end flickers.
VuMetersEffect.attribution: MoonLight original, on the VU ballistics of IEC 60268-17

damping.line: How much the needle overshoots; high is a studio meter.

response.line: How hard the needle chases the signal at all.

peakHold.line: How long the peak marker stays up, as a half-life.

smooth.line: Drive from the meter ballistic rather than the raw band.

BeatRipplesEffect.line: Every beat is a stone dropped in water.
BeatRipplesEffect.summary: A real wave simulation, which gives what a drawn expanding circle cannot: ripples pass through each other, reflect off the walls and interfere into standing patterns. The loudest band decides where the stone lands, a bass hit near the center and a treble hit out at the rim, and its strength sets how deep.
BeatRipplesEffect.attribution: the two-buffer water simulation (Gomez 2000) the demoscene settled on, here driven by the onset detector.

damping.line: How long the water keeps ringing.

drop.line: How deep a beat's stone falls.

rain.line: Idle drops when there is no music, so the surface is alive in silence.

shine.line: How strongly the slope lights the surface.

BlurzEffect.line: Audio-reactive blurred dots: one frequency band per frame lights a dot whose position maps to that band (or to the major-peak frequency), then the whole frame is blurred for soft trails.
BlurzEffect.attribution: WLED (audio) · by Andrew Tuline (WLED-SR), enhancements by [@softhack007](https://github.com/softhack007) · via [MoonLight](https://github.com/ewowi/MoonLight/blob/main/src/MoonLight/Nodes/Effects/E_WLED.h)

freqMap.line: Place the dot by the major-peak frequency, not by scanning.

geqScanner.line: Scan the dot across the strip in a GEQ-like sweep.

BouncingBallsEffect.line: A row of balls per column bounce under gravity, each losing energy on impact and relaunching when it stops, palette-colored by ball index over a fading background.

grav.line: Gravity strength (higher = faster fall, snappier bounce).

DemoReelEffect.line: Plays every other registered effect in turn, auto-advancing on a timer, so one Layer cycles the whole library hands-free.
DemoReelEffect.summary: New effects are picked up automatically. It can pick a fresh palette each cycle and overlay the playing effect's name, and the status line says which is playing. It never hosts itself, and it plays in sequence rather than compositing.

interval.line: Seconds each effect plays before advancing.

shuffle.line: Jump to a random next effect instead of registry order.

randomPalette.line: Pick a random palette on each cycle.

showName.line: Overlay the playing effect's name in a small font.

DistortionWavesEffect.line: Two interfering sine waves beat against each other into a moiré color field.
DistortionWavesEffect.attribution: WLED · by ldirko & blazoncek (WLED port) · [gallery](https://editor.soulmatelights.com/gallery/1089-distorsion-waves) · via [MoonLight](https://github.com/ewowi/MoonLight/blob/main/src/MoonLight/Nodes/Effects/E_WLED.h)

speed.line: Animation rate (0 = frozen).

FireEffect.line: A Fire2012-style heat field: sparks at the base rise and cool through the active palette, coldest at its low end.
FireEffect.summary:
The spark count scales with the width.

The flame color comes from the **active palette**. For the classic fire look pick the **Lava** palette (black→red→orange→yellow→white: the recommended default); any palette works, so an Ocean or Forest palette turns the flame blue or green.
FireEffect.attribution: FastLED / MoonLight · Mark Kriegsman's Fire2012; MoonLight adapts [MatrixFireFast](https://github.com/toggledbits/MatrixFireFast) (toggledbits)

cooling.line: How fast heat dissipates as it rises (higher = shorter flames).

sparking.line: Chance of a new spark at the base each frame; higher is livelier.

FixedRectangleEffect.line: A solid color filling a positioned box within the grid, with an optional alternating-white checker on the box's pixels.

Rectangle width.line: The box extent on each axis.

alternateWhite.line: Alternate box pixels to white in a checker pattern.

FreqMatrixEffect.line: A 1D scrolling frequency display: each frame shifts the strip and injects a new pixel at one end whose hue comes from the dominant frequency and whose brightness from the volume.

speed.line: Scroll rate.

lowBin.line: The frequency window mapped across the hue range.

highBin.line: The frequency window mapped across the hue range.

audioSpeed.line: Let the volume modulate the scroll speed.

FreqSawsEffect.line: Audio-reactive sawtooth waves: each column maps to a frequency band whose magnitude drives a per-band oscillator speed, so louder bands sweep their sawtooth up the column faster, with three phase methods.

increaser.line: How fast a band's speed ramps up with its magnitude.

decreaser.line: How fast a silent band's speed decays.

bpmMax.line: Ceiling on a band's oscillation speed.

keepOn.line: Keep oscillating even when a band is silent.

GameOfLifeEffect.line: Conway's cellular automaton generalized to 2D and 3D, with selectable rulesets and custom `B#/S#`.
GameOfLifeEffect.summary: Cells inherit a neighbor's palette color on birth, dead cells blur toward the background, and the board wraps toroidally. A stasis check respawns a pentomino or glider when the board goes static.
GameOfLifeEffect.attribution: MoonModules · by Ewoud Wijma (2022), mods by Brandon Butler / [@Brandon502](https://github.com/Brandon502) · [natureofcode](https://natureofcode.com/book/chapter-7-cellular-automata/) · via [MoonLight](https://github.com/ewowi/MoonLight/blob/main/src/MoonLight/Nodes/Effects/E_MoonModules.h)

backgroundColorR.line: The color dead cells fade toward.

ruleset.line: The birth and survive rule: Conway, HighLife, Maze and others.

customRuleString.line: A custom `B#/S#` rule, read only when `ruleset` = Custom.

mutationChance.line: % chance a newborn gets a random color.

disablePause.line: Skip the 1.5 s settle pause between boards.

colorByAge.line: Age from green to red, not a neighbor's palette color.

infinite.line: Respawn on stasis (R-pentomino/glider) instead of resetting.

blur.line: Dead-cell fade strength toward the background color.

GEQEffect.line: A flat graphic equaliser: the 16 audio bands rise as vertical bars from the bottom, with optional smoothing between bars, per-bar palette coloring, and falling peak markers.

fadeOut.line: How fast bars fade each frame.

colorBars.line: Color each bar from the palette by band instead of by row.

smoothBars.line: Blend neighboring bands for smoother bar heights.

GEQ3DEffect.line: A 3D-perspective graphic equaliser: audio bands rise as bars with faked depth, their side/top lines drawn toward a "projector" vanishing point (sweeping left↔right) and shortened by `depth`.
GEQ3DEffect.summary: Bands left of the projector are painted right-to-left, bands right of it left-to-right; per-face darkening (side/top/front) and optional `borders`.

speed.line: Projector sweep rate.

horizon.line: Vanishing-point row the projector sits on.

depth.line: How far the side/top perspective lines reach toward the projector.

numBands.line: Bands shown, fewer for wider bars.

LavaLampEffect.line: Three slow blobs through a black→red→orange→yellow→white ramp: atmospheric lava look.

intensity.line: Field gain into the black→red→orange→yellow→white ramp.

LinesEffect.line: Sweeps axis-aligned planes in sync; red/green/blue name the X/Y/Z axis: a preview-orientation test pattern.

mode.line: `lines` sweeps a plane, `panel dots` walks a dot per panel.

speed.line: Sweep BPM, in `lines`.

panelW.line: The panel the dot walks, in `panel dots`.

panelH.line: The panel the dot walks, in `panel dots`.

LissajousEffect.line: A Lissajous curve traced across the grid from two phase-shifted `sin8`/`cos8` sweeps, palette-colored along its length, with a fading trail.

xFrequency.line: The x-axis sweep frequency (sets the curve's lobe count).

speed.line: How fast the curve's phase advances.

MetaballsEffect.line: `count` blobs orbit via integer sin/cos; metaball field per pixel: bright HSV merge/split.

MoonLiveEffect.line: An effect you write as text on the running device, compiled to native code on the next tick.
MoonLiveEffect.summary:
Pick a script from the library or write your own, and it renders at the speed of a compiled effect. The language is [MoonLive](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/light/moonlive.html).

Every control the script declares, editable live without a recompile.
MoonLiveEffect.attribution: MoonLight original, on the native-codegen approach of [ESPLiveScript](https://github.com/hpwit/ESPLiveScript) by Yves Bazin

script.line: Which `.mle` file runs, picked from the library and edited here.

NetworkReceiveEffect.line: Receives lights over UDP into the layer, from Resolume, Madrix, xLights and LedFx.
NetworkReceiveEffect.summary:
Sender mapping is one copy alone on its layer, else two mappings, as the status shows. Behind a correcting sender, keep the profile in byte order, brightness 255 and the linear curve.

Listens for Art-Net, E1.31 and DDP at once. The end-to-end pair with [Network Send](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/light/drivers.html).

universe_start.line: The first incoming universe to map, mirroring the sender.

channels_per_universe.line: Bytes each universe maps to; 510 or 512.

mapped_by.line: **receiver** (sent row by row) or **sender** (in wiring order).

packets_per_s.line: Packets received in the last second, read-only.

frames_per_s.line: Frames received in the last second, read-only.

NoiseEffect.line: A gradient-noise field indexed straight into the palette: the plainest way to turn the field into light, and the effect every other noise effect is a variation on.
NoiseEffect.attribution: FastLED · inoise field (Mark Kriegsman); the `morph` form from WLED via [MoonLight](https://github.com/ewowi/MoonLight/blob/main/src/MoonLight/Nodes/Effects/E_WLED.h)

motion.line: `drift` slides the field across the fixture, `morph` changes it.

scale.line: Spatial frequency: low is broad blobs, high is fine detail.

NoiseMeterEffect.line: An audio VU meter rendered as a noise bar: the volume sets how many rows light from the bottom, each row colored by drifting Perlin noise, filling the full width and depth.

width.line: How strongly the volume drives the bar height.

PaintBrushEffect.line: Audio-reactive brush strokes: lines whose 3D endpoints oscillate on the beat (`beatsin8`, audio-band timebase), each stroke shortened to a band-magnitude length so the moving tip sweeps a curve over the fading field.

fadeRate.line: Background decay per frame, higher for shorter strokes.

minLength.line: A stroke draws only if longer than this, so quiet bands stay off.

color_chaos.line: Per-line random hue vs a per-band gradient.

ParticlesEffect.line: A swarm of drifting particles with persistent fading trails.

speed.line: Drift velocity.

FseqPlayerEffect.line: An FSEQ show played from a file: the frame-by-frame channel data xLights and Falcon Player write.
FseqPlayerEffect.summary: A show, uncompressed FSEQ v2, lands where a sender-mapped [Network Receive](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/light/effects.html#networkreceive) stream does, so alone on its layer it reaches the lights in one copy on any layout. Reading the file is the next step, and its status says so.
FseqPlayerEffect.attribution: FSEQ v2 as Falcon Player documents it in FSEQ_Sequence_File_Format.txt.
FseqPlayerEffect.alt: The reference sweep fseq_play writes, the show an FSEQ player plays

file.line: The show's path, an `.fseq` file on flash or under `/sd`.

speed.line: The playback speed, in percent of the file's step time.

PictureEffect.line: The active [Picture service](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/core/services.html#picture)'s picture on the layer, so a picture of any size shows on a layout of any size.
PictureEffect.summary: A modifier rotates, mirrors or tiles it as it does any effect, and a cube shows it on every slice.

fit.line: Keep the aspect with bands or cropped, or stretch it to the grid.
fit.more: **fit** shows the whole picture, with bands where its aspect leaves the grid empty. With **fill** it covers the grid and crops what overflows, and **stretch** distorts it to the grid's aspect.

sampling.line: One pixel per light, or the mean of the light's rectangle.
sampling.more: **point** takes the one pixel at a light's center, sharp and the fastest. With **area** each light averages its rectangle of the picture, so fine detail stays steady when a large picture shrinks onto few lights.

PlasmaEffect.line: Summed sine waves on orthogonal + diagonal axes; large rolling blobs (3D on volumetric layouts).

scale_x.line: Blob size on each axis; larger is bigger and calmer.

scale_y.line: Blob size on each axis; larger is bigger and calmer.

PraxisEffect.line: An algorithmic palette pattern driven by two beat oscillators (a macro and a micro mutator) whose frequencies and ranges reshape the hue field over time.

speed.line: How fast the pattern advances.

macroMutatorFreq.line: The coarse mutator's beat rate and range.

microMutatorFreq.line: The fine mutator's beat rate and range.

PulseEffect.line: Shells expanding from a drifting origin, one per beat: a pair of fronts on a strip, a ring on a panel, a sphere in a volume.
PulseEffect.summary:
Sound fires one and its pitch colors it, and an idle clock keeps them arriving in a silent room. The effect a device boots with.

Compare with [BeatRipples](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/light/effects.html#beatripples), which simulates water on a plane. This one draws a moving front, which carries it into 1D and 3D.

bpm.line: Pulses a minute while nothing is heard, where 0 waits for sound alone.

speed.line: How fast a shell crosses the layout, at any layout size.

thickness.line: The shell's width, as a share of the layout rather than in lights.

audioGain.line: How strongly sound fires a pulse, where 0 ignores it.

drift.line: How far the origin wanders from the center, where 0 pins it there.

RainbowEffect.line: Diagonal animated rainbow: always-visible default/test effect.

speed.line: Animation BPM (one full hue cycle per beat).

RandomEffect.line: Lights one random light per frame in a random palette color over a fading background: a sparse, palette-tinted sparkle.

fade.line: How fast prior sparkles fade to black.

RingsEffect.line: Expanding concentric rings from random centers, additive overlap (calm defaults).

speed.line: Expansion rate.

RipplesEffect.line: Distance-from-center sets a per-column wave phase; the lit surface ripples like water.

speed.line: Wave animation rate (0 = frozen, 99 = fast).

interval.line: Wavefront spacing (low = tight rings, high = wide).

RubiksCubeEffect.line: A 3D Rubik's Cube projected onto the volume: it scrambles, then plays its solution back one turn at a time, the six faces in their standard colors.

cubeSize.line: The cube order, its side in cells.

randomTurning.line: Turn endlessly at random instead of scramble-then-solve.

usePalette.line: Color the faces from the palette, not the classic colors.

SineEffect.line: R/G/B each follow a sine along one axis at 120° phase offset: a glowing, scrolling color box.

frequency.line: Spatial frequency, waves across the box.

SolidEffect.line: A flat fill with five color modes: a plain RGB(W) color, the active palette spread across the lights, an RMS-averaged single palette color, or the palette banded along the grid's rows or columns.

brightness.line: Scales the flat and palette-spread output.

colorMode.line: Flat `RGB(W)`, or the palette spread, averaged, or banded.

minRGB.line: In the band modes, drop palette entries darker than this floor.

randomColors.line: In the band modes, shuffle the surviving palette entries.

SdfShapesEffect.line: A circle and a box orbit and melt into each other, drawn as signed distance fields rather than outlines.
SdfShapesEffect.summary:
One distance per pixel yields three looks at once: a smooth fill, an outline, and a glow falling off into the field.

Measured on an ESP32-S3 at 128×128: 20 fps, 728 cycles/pixel using the true-distance form, alongside StarSky (692) and Metaballs (647) at the same size.
SdfShapesEffect.attribution: MoonLight original, after Iñigo Quilez's distance-function catalog and polynomial smooth-minimum (iquilezles.org)

radius.line: Circle radius, as a fraction of the short side.

blend.line: Melt radius; 0 unions the shapes hard.

outline.line: 0 fills the shape; higher draws an outline of that width.

glow.line: Tint the field around the shape by distance.

AuroraEffect.line: Several noise fields, each on its own clock, read in polar coordinates and composited into curtains of light.
AuroraEffect.summary: Nothing is simulated: layers of one field at different scales interfere, and that is what reads as curtains folding through one another. The strongest layer at each pixel wins, so they stay distinct rather than averaging into haze.
AuroraEffect.attribution: MoonLight original, in the shader vocabulary Stefan Petrick made recognizable in the LED world

speed.line: Master rate; every layer scales from it, and 0 freezes it.

scale.line: Noise cells across the grid; low is broad, high is fine.

layers.line: How many fields are composited, and the main cost knob.

warp.line: How far the field displaces its own angle, folding a curtain over.

twist.line: How much the radius shears the angle, giving the curtains their lean.

segments.line: Kaleidoscope wedges; 1 leaves the composition unfolded.

contrast.line: How much of the field lights; low is cloud, high is sharp.

octaves.line: Detail within each layer, multiplying the cost knob.

PolarNoiseEffect.line: A warped noise field addressed by angle and radius, folded into a kaleidoscope.
PolarNoiseEffect.summary:
The field turns and breathes around the center rather than scrolling past it.

Cost scales with `octaves` and `warp`: at `warp` > 0 and `octaves` 2 it is roughly 4 noise samples per pixel. On a large wall set `octaves` to 1 or `warp` to 0, which degrades to a plain polar noise that still reads well.
PolarNoiseEffect.attribution: MoonLight original, after Stefan Petrick's polar/noise vocabulary and Iñigo Quilez's domain warping

scale.line: Noise cells across the grid; low is broad, high is fine detail.

warp.line: Domain-warp strength; 0 gives a plain field.

octaves.line: Fbm octaves, and the main cost knob.

twist.line: How much the radius shears the angle, setting the spiral.

WaterRippleEffect.line: A propagating wave simulation: drops land, their rings spread outward, reflect off the edges and interfere where they cross.
WaterRippleEffect.summary:
The crossing is what a drawn ripple cannot fake, because two rings meeting have to add and cancel.

Distinct from [Ripples](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/light/effects.html#ripples), which draws clean concentric circles; this behaves like water.
WaterRippleEffect.attribution: MoonLight original, on Hugo Elias's water surface algorithm

speed.line: Simulation steps per second: how fast the water itself moves.

dropRate.line: How often drops land, in time rather than per frame.

damping.line: How fast waves lose energy; higher is calmer water.

colorByHeight.line: Color by height, so crests and troughs read differently.

hueBase.line: Where the still surface sits, and how far waves go.

hueSpread.line: Where the still surface sits, and how far waves go.

FluidEffect.line: Light poured into a simulated medium and carried by it.
FluidEffect.summary:
Every other flow here is a function of position and time; this one is state, so a jet fired now changes where everything downstream goes for seconds afterwards.

On a cube every depth slice is its own medium, so the slices differ. Sized for the desktop and the P4.

jets.line: How many places light is poured in.

force.line: How hard each one pushes the medium.

swirl.line: How fast the jets sweep, which is what stirs vortices.

viscosity.line: How much the medium drags on itself; high is syrup, low smoke.

persistence.line: How long dye survives, as a half-life.

iterations.line: Pressure-solve effort, and the cost knob.

NebulaEffect.line: A noise field decides where light is born, a curl flow decides where it goes, and between them the cloud keeps folding into itself.
NebulaEffect.summary:
The emitter is a field rather than a handful of dots, so light enters everywhere at once and the flow shapes a whole cloud instead of drawing trails.

Held at 16 bits and dithered on the way out, which keeps a slow fade smooth.
NebulaEffect.attribution: MoonLight original, composing the noise-field and curl-flow kernels: the contrast window is Aurora's, in the shader vocabulary Stefan Petrick made recognizable in the LED world, and the flow is Bridson's curl noise (SIGGRAPH 2007)

speed.line: How fast the medium moves, and with it the whole cloud.

scale.line: The field's cell size; low is broad clouds, high is wisps.

contrast.line: What fraction of the field is bright enough to be born.

persistence.line: How long light survives once it is in the flow, as a half-life.

octaves.line: Detail within the field, and its cost knob.

fieldScale.line: Compute the field at half or quarter resolution and stretch it.

fieldRate.line: Recompute the field every N frames; the flow still runs each one.

TrailsEffect.line: Dots thrown into a moving medium, leaving tails the flow carries and bends.
TrailsEffect.summary:
Nothing draws a tail: it is the previous frames' dots, transported along a velocity field and dimmed, which is why the flow's shape is visible in it. On a cube each depth slice gets its own flow.

The trail plane is 16-bit, which is what lets a tail fade smoothly rather than stepping.
TrailsEffect.attribution: MoonLight original, in the flow-field idiom (4wheeljive's FlowFields, from a Stefan Petrick concept), with Stam's backward advection for the transport

speed.line: How fast the medium moves, and with it every tail.

dots.line: How many emitters are throwing light in.

scale.line: The flow field's cell size; low is broad sweeps, high is eddies.

persistence.line: How long a tail survives, as a half-life.

breathe.line: How much the flow's strength rises and falls.

ColorTrailsEffect.line: Emitters pouring color into a flow that carries and folds it.
ColorTrailsEffect.summary:
There is no velocity field: one noise value shifts each row sideways, one shifts each column, and the two shears compose into a swirling current. A large grid is steered by a few hundred numbers, which is why it runs where a solver does not.

Compare with [Fluid](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/light/effects.html#fluid): the solver when the medium is the subject, this when the color is.
ColorTrailsEffect.attribution: MoonLight · concept by [Stefan Petrick](https://github.com/StefanPetrick), composition by Jeff (mindful_stone / [4wheeljive](https://github.com/4wheeljive)) in [FlowFields](https://github.com/4wheeljive/FlowFields/blob/main/src/flows/flow_noise.h) · via [MoonLight](https://github.com/ewowi/MoonLight/blob/main/src/MoonLight/Nodes/Effects/E_FastLED.h)

speed.line: How fast the emitters travel.

flow.line: How far a row or column is pushed: the shear amount.

flowSpeed.line: How fast the flow itself drifts and reverses.

scale.line: The profiles' spatial frequency: a few broad bands or many fine ones.

persistence.line: How long color survives, as a half-life.

colorSpeed.line: How fast the emitters walk the palette.

size.line: The orbit's radius and the Lissajous figure's reach.

mode.line: All three emitters, or one at a time to see what each contributes.

flowType.line: The field carrying them: `Noise`, `Radial out`, `Radial in`.

TunnelEffect.line: A texture mapped onto the inside of an infinite tube, so the viewer appears to fly down it forever.
TunnelEffect.summary: Nothing is 3D: the angle around the center is one texture coordinate and the reciprocal of the distance is the other, which is perspective for the price of a divide.
TunnelEffect.attribution: MoonLight original, on the standard demoscene tunnel

bpm.line: How fast the tunnel flies past.

depth.line: Texture scale along the tunnel; higher is finer rings.

twist.line: Rotation per unit depth, so the tunnel corkscrews.

segments.line: Kaleidoscope the wall; 1 leaves it plain.

octaves.line: Wall texture detail, and the cost knob.

vignette.line: Darken toward the vanishing point so it reads as receding.

EchoEffect.line: The previous frame fed back through a zoom and rotation, dimmed, with a bright source drawn on top: trails that spiral away from themselves, like a camera pointed at its own monitor.
EchoEffect.summary: Shows that feedback is not a primitive: once the grid can be read as a texture (`sampleWrap`), the whole family of trails, zoom blur and smear is a few lines.
EchoEffect.attribution: MoonLight original, on video feedback and the standard texture-feedback shader shape

zoom.line: How much the feedback grows each frame.

rotate.line: Rotation per frame, which turns the trail into a spiral.

decay.line: How fast the echo fades; higher is a shorter trail.

DissolveEffect.line: Two color fields trade places pixel by pixel in an order that looks random but is computed, so the transition needs no per-pixel state and no shuffled index list.
DissolveEffect.summary: Two devices rendering the same frame dissolve identically without exchanging anything.
DissolveEffect.attribution: MoonLight original, on the classic dissolve transition in its position-addressed (shader) form

spread.line: How long pixels spend mid-flight; 0 gives a hard edge.

eased.line: Ease the progress instead of sweeping linearly.

scatter.line: Random order; off gives a positional wipe from the same code.

SpectrumEffect.line: An audio analyzer with real meter ballistics: bars rise fast enough to catch a transient and fall slowly enough to read, and a peak dot marks the recent maximum and drifts down.
SpectrumEffect.summary: The asymmetry is the whole point; a symmetric follower either misses the hit or flickers.
SpectrumEffect.attribution: MoonLight original, on standard VU/PPM meter ballistics and WLED's GEQ band mapping

attack.line: How fast a bar rises toward a new level.

peakDecay.line: How fast the peak dot drifts down.

colorByColumn.line: Color per band instead of by height.

FireworksEffect.line: Shells rise, stall, and burst into sparks that arc over and fall.
FireworksEffect.summary:
Nothing schedules the apex: the shell decelerates under gravity and bursts when its vertical velocity crosses zero, so a faster launch bursts higher without a second control.

Physics runs on elapsed time, so the same settings behave identically at any frame rate.
FireworksEffect.attribution: MoonLight original, on the WLED Particle System's firework family by Damian Schneider / [@DedeHai](https://github.com/DedeHai)

launchRate.line: How often a new shell goes up.

launchSpeed.line: How hard it is thrown, and so how high it bursts.

gravity.line: How fast everything falls, per 60 Hz of simulated time.

fade.line: Trail length (the Layer's decay, not the pool's).

FishTankEffect.line: An aquarium on a light wall: fish of three shapes swim across a dark tank, each in its own color from the active palette, tails beating.
FishTankEffect.summary:
The art carries shade roles rather than fixed colors, and each fish fills them from its own place on the palette, so one drawing yields as many colorways as there are fish.

Uses the global palette, each fish's band a paler version of its own body color.
FishTankEffect.attribution: MoonLight original; inspired by the aquarium screensavers of the After Dark era, the pixel art drawn fresh for this effect

speed.line: Swim rate in body-lengths, the same on any grid.

spriteSize.line: Integer magnification; 0 is auto, scaling with the grid.

audioReactive.line: Each sprite follows its own band, so the scene breathes.

PacmanEffect.line: The arcade cast crossing a light wall: Pacman chomps his way along while the four ghosts drift past, each in its own color, wrapping around the edges forever.
PacmanEffect.summary:
The characters travel independently, each on its own path.

Pacman keeps his yellow; the ghosts take their colors from the active palette.
PacmanEffect.attribution: MoonLight original; inspired by Namco's Pac-Man (1980), the pixel art drawn fresh for this effect

ghosts.line: How many ghosts (0-8); the arcade cast is four.

speed.line: Travel rate in sprite-widths, the same on any grid.

spriteSize.line: Integer magnification; 0 is auto, scaling with the grid.

audioReactive.line: Each sprite follows its own band, so the scene breathes.

FixedPointEffect.line: Shapes placed between pixels rather than on them.
FixedPointEffect.summary:
A clock hand drawn on whole pixels jumps a pixel at a time and reads as broken; the same hand at a fractional position moves smoothly, because a pixel's brightness carries the fraction its position cannot.

Eleven figures, from a geared clock through a spirograph to boids and a swaying tree.

demo.line: Which figure, or `all` to cycle them.

bpm.line: How fast the orbits and curves run; the clock keeps its own.

fade.line: How much of the previous frame survives, which leaves the trail.

dwell.line: Seconds each demo holds before `all` moves on.

drift.line: How far the scene wanders from center, in pixels; 0 pins it.

zoom.line: The camera pushes in and settles back; 0 holds it fixed.

MovingHeadEffect.line: Aims a rig of moving heads as one instrument.
MovingHeadEffect.summary:
Pan and tilt sweep at different rates, so a beam traces a path rather than a line, and `formation` decides how the heads relate.

The first effect that aims a fixture rather than only coloring it.

**fan**, **mirror**, **chase**, **cross** and **unison**.

A fixture chain is one-dimensional, so lay the rig out as a **1 x N** grid.

panBpm.line: Sweep rates. Differing rates trace a path, not a line.

tiltBpm.line: Sweep rates. Differing rates trace a path, not a line.

panRange.line: How much of the fixture's travel to use.

tiltRange.line: How much of the fixture's travel to use.

panCenter.line: Where the sweep is centered; 128 is the middle.

tiltCenter.line: Where the sweep is centered; 128 is the middle.

audioReactive.line: The beam widens with the room, each head on its own band.

gobo.line: The beam's wheels, as raw bytes; see the manual.

rotate.line: The beam's wheels, as raw bytes; see the manual.

goboOnBeat.line: Roll a new gobo on a bass hit, then hold it a moment.

FlyingToastersEffect.line: The classic screensaver on a light wall: chrome toasters with flapping wings and slices of toast drift diagonally across the dark, forever.
FlyingToastersEffect.summary:
The wing flap carries a per-toaster offset, so the flock never falls into sync.

The sprites carry their own colors (chrome, wing, crust), so the global palette does not apply. Needs a grid at least the toaster's size (12×9).
FlyingToastersEffect.attribution: MoonLight original; inspired by After Dark's Flying Toasters (Berkeley Systems, 1989), suggested by [troyhacks](https://github.com/troyhacks): the pixel art here is drawn fresh for this effect

speed.line: Drift rate in sprite-widths, the same on any grid.

spriteSize.line: Integer magnification for toasters and toast; 0 is auto.

audioReactive.line: Each sprite follows its own band, so the scene breathes.

SpaceInvadersEffect.line: The 1978 formation marching down the wall: five ranks stepping sideways in the two-frame wiggle, dropping a row and reversing at each wall, and speeding up as the ranks thin.
SpaceInvadersEffect.summary:
That acceleration is the defining mechanic. Invaders fire down, the cannon fires back, and a landing resets the board.

The invaders take their body color from the active palette.
SpaceInvadersEffect.attribution: MoonLight original, after Taito's Space Invaders (1978)

marchBpm.line: Steps per minute when full; it speeds up as the ranks thin.

stepX.line: How far a step moves the formation sideways, in pixels.

dropY.line: How far a wall turn drops it, in pixels.

size.line: Magnification per art pixel; 1 on a matrix, 2 or more on a wall.

audioReactive.line: The formation steps on transients, locking to the track.

player.line: The cannon, for a fader or an input; idle, the game plays it.

fire.line: A button that fires the cannon, one shot in the air at a time.

SpriteFountainEffect.line: A fountain that throws the project's whole sprite cast: fish, Pacman and his ghosts, toasters and toast, and the three invaders, launched from the floor on a sweeping nozzle and falling back under gravity.
SpriteFountainEffect.summary:
The art is shared with the effects that introduced it, so a fix to a fish fixes it in both places.

Colors come from the active palette, one per sprite, held for its whole flight.

lift.line: How hard the nozzle throws; it scales with the grid.

pull.line: Gravity. 3 gives a two-second arc, long enough to read a toaster.

rate.line: Sprites launched per beat of the emit clock.

emitBpm.line: Launches per minute, so the plume's density is a choice.

audioReactive.line: One sprite per band, so the cast maps onto the spectrum.

PongEffect.line: Two paddles rallying a ball, the attract mode of the 1972 original where both players are the machine.
PongEffect.summary:
A perfect tracker would rally forever and never look like a game, so each paddle has a reaction delay and a small aiming error, re-rolled every exchange. That is what produces the occasional point. The score shows at the top, and the first to 11 starts a new game.

Uses the global palette.

rallyBpm.line: Ball crossings per minute, the same time on any grid.

paddle.line: Length as a percentage of the court; short paddles miss more.

reflex.line: How sharply a paddle chases. Below full it lags a fast ball.

spriteBall.line: Swap the square for a sprite, re-picked on every hit.

size.line: Integer magnification of the sprite ball, shown while it is on.

player1.line: The left paddle's height, for a fader or input; idle, the game plays.

player2.line: The right paddle, the same way.

BreakoutEffect.line: A paddle knocking down a wall of bricks, the attract mode of the 1976 original where the machine plays itself.
BreakoutEffect.summary:
The paddle waits out a reaction delay and aims slightly off, so steep balls outrun it. The ball speeds up as bricks fall, and the paddle halves once the ball reaches the back wall. Three misses, or a cleared wall, deal a fresh one.

The brick rows take their colors from the active palette.

speedBpm.line: Court crossings per minute at the serve, the same time on any grid.

rows.line: Rows of bricks, fewer where the grid has no room.

paddle.line: Width as a percentage of the court.

reflex.line: How sharply the paddle chases. Below full it lags a steep ball.

descend.line: The wall creeps down and new rows enter at the top.

audioReactive.line: Columns glow with their bands, the palette follows the volume.

player.line: The paddle, for a fader or an input; idle, the game plays it.

BallpitEffect.line: Falling balls that pile up and shove each other aside.
BallpitEffect.summary:
The heap is emergent: gravity pulls, the floor stops, and contact between neighbors makes the shape. `tilt` turns the pit into a slope and the pile slides and re-settles.

Collisions are the one non-linear part of the particle kernel, so the pool is small.
BallpitEffect.attribution: MoonLight original, on the WLED Particle System's ballpit family by Damian Schneider / [@DedeHai](https://github.com/DedeHai)

size.line: Contact radius in pixels: how far apart balls sit when touching.

bounce.line: Restitution: how much speed a contact keeps.

tilt.line: Sideways force, turning the pit into a slope.

drag.line: Damping, so the heap settles instead of sloshing.

TruchetEffect.line: A maze of interlocking arcs that never repeats, drawn without storing a single tile.
TruchetEffect.summary:
Randomly turned tiles join into continuous winding paths across the surface: the pattern looks designed, and nothing designed it.

**The representative 2D shader**: no 3D, no rays, no float, and cheap on any target.
TruchetEffect.attribution: MoonLight original, on Sébastien Truchet's 1704 tiling and the standard shader fract/hash/smoothstep idiom

shuffle.line: Reshuffles which way the tiles face.

drift.line: Slide the pattern instead of holding still.

VectorBallsEffect.line: A rotating 3D object drawn as shaded spheres, the demoscene classic that named the technique.
VectorBallsEffect.summary:
The smallest complete demonstration of putting 3D on a panel: rotate, project, sort back to front, shade by distance, draw.

Without painter's ordering a far ball paints over a near one and the object turns inside out.
VectorBallsEffect.attribution: MoonLight original, on the Amiga-era demoscene vector-ball effect

size.line: Ball radius at the object's center, in pixels.

spread.line: How far apart the balls sit.

distance.line: How far the object is from the viewer.

fade.line: Dim the far balls, which is what reads as depth.

RaymarchEffect.line: A lit 3D scene rendered by marching a ray through a distance field, one ray per pixel.
RaymarchEffect.summary:
Nothing draws a sphere: the scene is a function returning the distance to the nearest surface, and the spheres emerge where each ray stops.

Compiled only where the chip has a hardware FPU. Cost is per pixel, so `steps` trades quality against it.
RaymarchEffect.attribution: MoonLight original, on Iñigo Quilez's raymarching and distance-function articles

steps.line: Ray marching steps: the quality and cost knob.

blend.line: How much the two spheres melt into each other.

SphereMoveEffect.line: A hollow spherical shell that bounces through the 3D volume, its surface colored from the palette, leaving no trail.

speed.line: How fast the sphere moves through the volume.

twist.line: How tightly the arm winds (hue gain per unit of distance).

StarFieldEffect.line: A perspective starfield: stars approach the viewer from a vanishing point, brightening as they near, then respawn at depth.
StarFieldEffect.attribution: MoonLight · by [@Brandon502](https://github.com/Brandon502), inspired by Daniel Shiffman / [Coding Train](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=17WoOqgXsRM) · via [MoonLight](https://github.com/ewowi/MoonLight/blob/main/src/MoonLight/Nodes/Effects/E_MoonLight.h)

speed.line: How fast stars approach (frame throttle).

usePalette.line: Color the stars from the palette instead of white.

StarSkyEffect.line: Twinkling stars at random light positions, each fading in and out independently over a dark background.

speed.line: Fade rate per frame (how fast each star brightens/dims).

star_fill_ratio.line: How many stars (as a fraction of the light count).

usePalette.line: Color the stars from the active palette instead of white.

TetrixEffect.line: Falling Tetris-style blocks: each column drops a brick that lands on the growing stack, fills the column, then clears and restarts.

speed.line: Fall speed (0 = randomised per brick).

oneColor.line: One advancing palette color for every brick, not one each.

TextEffect.line: Renders a multi-line string in a bitmap font.
TextEffect.summary: Static by default (laid out top-left, each newline dropping one font-height, clipped where it runs off the grid); turn on `scroll` to march the whole block leftwards as a wrapping marquee. Text color comes from the active palette.
TextEffect.attribution: MoonLight original, on MoonLight's Scrolling Text · via [MoonLight](https://github.com/ewowi/MoonLight/blob/main/src/MoonLight/Nodes/Effects/E_MoonLight.h)

text.line: The string to show; each line renders on its own row.

scroll.line: Off is static, on a horizontal marquee.

speed.line: Marquee speed (only used when `scroll` is on).

hue.line: Palette index for the text color.

WaveEffect.line: An oscilloscope waveform scrolls across the grid with a fading trail; six selectable shapes.

fade.line: Trail fade per frame (0 = instant clear, 255 = long tail).

waveform.line: Sawtooth, triangle, sine, square, sin3 or noise.

BlockModifier.line: Expands a 1D effect into concentric square rings: its position along the strip becomes the ring, so a gradient draws nested squares.
BlockModifier.summary: The square sibling of [Circle](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/light/modifiers.html#circle), which draws round rings.

CheckerboardModifier.line: Masks the layer in a checkerboard: the lights on the "off" squares stay dark, the rest show the effect unchanged.

size.line: The edge of a checker square, in lights.

invert.line: Swap which squares show the effect and which stay dark.

MoonLiveModifier.line: The coordinate transform written as text on the running device: mirror the pattern, shift it, swap its axes.
MoonLiveModifier.summary: A compiled modifier is a class and a reflash, where a script is a line of text applied as you type, and every control it declares appears on the card. The language is [MoonLive](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/light/moonlive.html).

guide.title: One coordinate at a time
guide.text:
A script transforms one coordinate and needs no loop, because the Layer already calls it once per physical light while it builds the mapping.

`setXYZ(x, y, z)` writes the transformed position, as `setRGB(index, r, g, b)` writes a color: a mirror is `void modifyLogical() { setXYZ(width - 1 - xPos, yPos, zPos); }`.

guide.title: Read the grid rather than assuming it
guide.text:
A mirror written against a fixed 255 sends every light of a 16-wide grid outside it. The Layer drops each one, and the fixture goes black with no error, because the script ran perfectly.

A computed coordinate is full width: `setXYZ` hands its values to the binding as a call, so `setXYZ(767 - xPos, ...)` on a 768-wide wall arrives as 767.

guide.title: What a script can transform
guide.text:
A modifier has two hooks: one reshapes the logical box once per rebuild, and one folds each coordinate. A script drives the second, so a transform keeping the box its size works, and one halving it, as the built-in Mirror does, needs the compiled modifier.

A script that fails to compile shows the parse error, and the mapping passes coordinates straight through, so the device keeps rendering until the script parses again.

script.line: Which `.mlm` script runs, picked from the library and edited here.

CircleModifier.line: Expands a 1D effect into concentric circular rings: its position along the strip becomes the radius, so a gradient draws nested circles.
CircleModifier.summary: The round sibling of [Block](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/light/modifiers.html#block), which draws square rings.

MirrorModifier.line: Folds the far half of the box back onto the near half, mirroring the image across its center on each axis you choose.
MirrorModifier.summary: In 2D one quadrant shows in all four, in 3D one octant in all eight.

mirrorX.line: Mirror across the center along x.

mirrorY.line: Mirror across the center along y.

mirrorZ.line: Mirror across the center along z.

MultiplyModifier.line: Tiles the image across the box, a number of times per axis, and can mirror every other tile into a kaleidoscope.
MultiplyModifier.summary: Two tiles with mirroring on is a plain mirror.

multiplyX.line: Tiles along x, one meaning none.

multiplyY.line: Tiles along y, one meaning none.

multiplyZ.line: Tiles along z, one meaning none.

mirrorX.line: Reflect every other tile along x.

mirrorY.line: Reflect every other tile along y.

mirrorZ.line: Reflect every other tile along z.

PinwheelModifier.line: Remaps the grid into petals around the center, so a line or a 2D effect turns into a rotating flower or spokes.
PinwheelModifier.summary: The angle to each light picks its petal, and the radius runs along it; swirl, symmetry and z-twist bend the pattern.

petals.line: How many petals radiate from the center.

swirl.line: How far a petal bends into a spiral, negative bending the other way.

symmetry.line: How many times the pattern repeats around the turn.

zTwist.line: How far the petals twist from one z layer to the next.

RandomMapModifier.line: Moves every light to another, each one exactly once, and reshuffles on a beat: the arrangement scrambles while the content stays.

bpm.line: Reshuffles per minute, zero freezing the arrangement.

RegionModifier.line: Crops the layer to a rectangle given in percentages of each axis, so it holds when the layout is resized; outside it is dark.
RegionModifier.summary: Beyond 0 and 100 the window slides partly or wholly out of view.

startX.line: Where the region starts along x, in percent of the axis.

startY.line: Where it starts along y, in percent.

startZ.line: Where it starts along z, in percent.

endX.line: Where the region ends along x, in percent of the axis.

endY.line: Where it ends along y, in percent.

endZ.line: Where it ends along z, in percent.

RippleXZModifier.line: Collapses an axis to a single plane, so an effect drawn along the other axes ripples across the whole box.

shrink.line: Collapse the chosen axes to a single plane.

towardsX.line: Collapse x, so each column shares one light.

towardsZ.line: Collapse z, so each x-y plane is shared across depth.

RotateModifier.line: Turns the 2D image around its center, continuously, at the speed you set.

speed.line: How fast the image turns.

TransposeModifier.line: Swaps a pair of axes and can flip each one, so the image rotates or mirrors without the effect redrawing.

XY.line: Swap x and y, rows becoming columns.

inverse X.line: Flip x after the swaps, so it reads back to front.

HueDriver.line: Drives **Philips Hue bulbs as pixels**: each color bulb in the driver's window becomes one pixel, pushed to the bridge over its HTTP API.
HueDriver.summary: Paced to the bridge's ~10 cmd/s limit, so smooth ambient color, not strobing. Up to 32 bulbs, which is a LAN's worth and bounds the driver's memory.

appKey.line: The Hue app key, filled by `pair`; a password, so masked and kept out of documents.

pair.line: Button: press it, then the bridge's physical link button within ~30 s to claim a key.

room.line: Dropdowns narrowing which color lights are driven.

light.line: Dropdowns narrowing which color lights are driven.

NetworkSendDriver.line: Streams the buffer over UDP as **Art-Net**, **E1.31 / sACN** or **DDP**, its packets paced so receivers keep up, to Falcon/Advatek controllers, xLights and LedFx.
NetworkSendDriver.summary: Feeds several receivers from one driver, each its own slice. Mixed DMX fixtures and the addressing rules are in [the details below](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/light/drivers.html#network-send-details).

guide.title: Network Send, details
guide.text: **Unicast is the default** because Art-Net 4 requires it and because broadcast makes every host on the LAN parse every packet; Art-Net's `broadcast` remains for legacy receivers. **E1.31 multicast** sends to sACN's own per-universe group (`239.255.{universe_hi}.{universe_lo}`) rather than to `hosts`, so one send reaches every receiver that joined that universe. It is opt-in rather than the default, because the saving only materializes on a switch that does IGMP snooping and firmware cannot tell. See [multicast and IGMP snooping](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/explanation/architecture/moonlight.html#multicast-and-igmp-snooping). On a network shown to drop multicast, the card says so rather than broadcasting every universe. A name in `hosts` resolves in the background, `.local` by mDNS and anything else by DNS: it sends nothing until it first resolves, keeps its last address while it stops answering, and the card says which names are still waiting. **A DMX chain of MIXED fixtures needs one driver per fixture type.** `lightsPerHost` splits a window between receivers that share one fixture profile, so it cannot describe a chain where the fixtures differ. Add a driver per type instead, each reading its own `start`/`count` slice of the same buffer with its own `fixture`. Two moving-head types followed by RGBW pars is three drivers: Each maps its slice onto that fixture's real channels, so differing channel counts and orders are fine, and each carries its own `universe_start`. The layout must hold every light, 16 here, since the windows are slices of one shared buffer. Two consequences of motion channels being a property of the LAYER rather than of a driver: **Order matters when the motion ROLES differ**, which is why the table puts the pan/tilt/zoom heads first. The layer's motion slots come from the first enabled driver whose profile carries motion, so the richest fixture has to lead. Swap A and B and the zoom has no slot at all, so those heads never zoom. Fixtures differing only in channel count or order are unaffected. **Every light carries the motion bytes**, used or not, so a mixed rig's buffer is as wide as its widest fixture. Memory rather than correctness: a par's `Correction` discards the aim. An effect writes `setPan` for every light in its layer, so a formation spanning the window treats the pars as rig positions too. Use separate **Layers** when the heads should move independently.

protocol.line: Art-Net / E1.31 / DDP; the port follows.

addressing.line: Unicast for all three, multicast for E1.31, broadcast for Art-Net.

hosts.line: The receivers, such as `192.168.1.70-74, panel-01.local`. **Blank idles.**

lightsPerHost.line: Lights per receiver. Blank splits evenly, one number to all, a list each.

universe_start.line: First universe for Art-Net / E1.31, restarting per receiver. DDP ignores it.

packet_gap.line: Μs between a frame's packets; 0 sends the frame as one burst.

PreviewDriver.line: Streams a true-shape 3D preview to the web UI as a **point list**, only the real lights at their real positions, so a sphere/ring/arbitrary map shows in its true shape.
PreviewDriver.summary:
The one boot-wired driver.

It streams on its own WebSocket channel so a large frame never delays the control plane, and only while a viewer is watching. Moving heads show their beam. How the rate and detail trade off is in [the details below](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/light/drivers.html#preview-details).

guide.title: Preview, details
guide.text: **Close the preview when you do not need it.** The device renders preview frames only while the preview pane is open. Dismissing it stops that work entirely, which frees the device for rendering and keeps the UI responsive on a large layout, worth doing while you are editing effects on a big wall. **The preview thins itself out.** When the connection cannot carry full detail, the preview shows a regular sample of the lights rather than all, the status reads `preview 1/4` and so on. The device reports every frame it had to drop and your browser reacts. Persistent drops trade detail for rate, drop-free stretches earn it back a step at a time, and a step that brings the drops back is undone with growing patience, so a borderline connection settles instead of flickering between sizes. A slow *effect* drops nothing, so it never costs preview detail. A fast connection previews everything, with nothing to configure. **If the preview looks choppy**, it is the connection rather than the device: frames are dropped rather than queued, so the wall itself is never held up by the preview. Lower `targetFps` if you would rather keep full detail at a slower rate.

targetFps.line: The rate to aim for. **Lower for detail, raise for smoothness.**

NdiDriver.line: Publishes the layer as an **NDI video source**, so OBS, Resolume, TouchDesigner or any other NDI receiver picks MoonLight up by name, on this machine or another on the network.
NdiDriver.summary:
Where the Preview driver draws the lights for a person, this hands the same frame to a production tool as video.

The grid becomes the frame, one light per pixel, output correction applied, so a receiver sees what the wall sees. **Desktop only, and you install the NDI runtime yourself**; without it the driver says so and nothing else changes. See [the details below](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/light/drivers.html#ndi-details).

guide.title: NDI, details
guide.text:
**You install the NDI runtime yourself**, MoonLight cannot ship it. Until you do, the driver reports `NDI runtime not installed` and everything else works normally.

**To see the output** you need a receiver. **NDI Video Monitor** (part of NDI Tools) is the simplest; OBS gains an "NDI Source" via the [DistroAV](https://github.com/DistroAV/DistroAV) plugin. MoonLight appears by the name in `sourceName`, or the device's own name when that is blank.

**Desktop only.** No NDI runtime exists for the ESP32 chips, so the driver is not offered there. An ESP32 reaches the same tools over Art-Net, sACN or DDP instead, send with the [Network Send](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/light/drivers.html#networksend) driver, receive with the NetworkReceive effect.

**Status line**

sourceName.line: The name a receiver lists. Blank uses the device's own name.

fps.line: Frame-rate ceiling, declared in every frame.

HlsDriver.line: Streams the layer as **H.264 over HLS** from the device's own HTTP server.
HlsDriver.summary:
Open the `url` the card shows in VLC or a browser, or hand it to an Apple TV. Where NDI feeds production tools, this feeds anything that plays video.

The grid becomes the frame, output correction applied. Latency is HLS's own, **2-5 seconds**, so this is for watching rather than live-control feedback. Runs on desktop (you install ffmpeg) and on the **ESP32-P4**, which encodes in hardware. See [the details below](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/light/drivers.html#hls-details).

read-only: `url` to play. The card's status line carries state, drops, or why the encoder stopped.

guide.title: HLS, details
guide.text: **On desktop you install ffmpeg yourself** (any 5.x+, on PATH), because MoonLight never ships or links an encoder. Install it with `brew` on macOS, `winget` on Windows, or `apt` on Debian, Ubuntu and Raspberry Pi OS. Without it the driver reports `ffmpeg not found` and nothing else changes. The `encoder` control picks which one ffmpeg uses: `libx264` (the default, in practically every build) is software. Three hardware encoders offload it instead, and are worth picking on large grids: `h264_videotoolbox` on a Mac (~10% CPU for a 1024x1024 stream on Apple Silicon), `h264_v4l2m2m` on a Raspberry Pi, and `h264_nvenc` on NVIDIA. An encoder your ffmpeg lacks starts and exits immediately; the status then reads `encoder exited - check ffmpeg`. **On the ESP32-P4** there is no ffmpeg and no filesystem in the path: the chip's own H.264 block encodes and MoonLight packages the MPEG-TS itself. Segments are served from a RAM ring rather than written to flash, which at one segment per second would wear it for nothing. The `encoder` control is absent, since the hardware offers only one. **Sizing the picture.** The P4's encoder takes only EVEN dimensions between 80x80 and 1920x2032, so an odd wall has its scale doubled so both axes come out even. A wall whose scaled size exceeds the maximum is refused with a status rather than streaming something the hardware cannot encode. Desktop ffmpeg has none of these limits. The floor is what the auto scale exists for: the P4 will not accept a frame smaller than 80x80, and a small wall streamed 1:1 arrives as a postage stamp in the player. `scale` at 0 (the default) therefore picks the smallest whole factor that lifts *both* axes to 80: a 20x10 wall streams as 160x80 rather than being refused, and a wall already past 80 stays 1:1. One factor serves both axes, so the aspect ratio is preserved and each light stays a square block. Raising `scale` by hand on an already-large wall costs real time (a 128x128 wall at scale 4 measures about 60 ms per frame against 1 ms at 1:1) and buys nothing a player's own zoom does not. **The bitrate is derived, not a setting.** It follows from the grid size and `targetFps` at about 0.1 bits per pixel per frame, which puts a 512x512 wall at 30 fps near 800 kbit; a 128x128 lands under the 500 kbit floor the derivation clamps to. `targetFps` is the knob for bandwidth, and the better trade for LED content: fewer frames rather than a blockier picture. **Where the segments live.** On desktop, the transient `/.hls/` directory, served at `/hls/` and excluded from config backups. Large grids trade framerate, the render loop being single-threaded: 512x512 streams smoothly, TV-native resolutions stutter.

targetFps.line: Encode-rate ceiling, and the bandwidth knob: bitrate follows.

scale.line: Video pixels per light (0 = auto). Each light is a solid block, never a blur.

RtspDriver.line: Streams the layer as **H.264 over RTSP**, which a player pulls rather than fetching segments.
RtspDriver.summary:
Point VLC or `ffplay` at the `url` the card shows. It reaches a viewer **much sooner than HLS**, which buffers whole segments before it plays one, so this is the remote view to reach for. [Preview](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/light/drivers.html#preview) stays the one that keeps pace with the lights, sending raw pixels and no codec at all.

Runs on the **ESP32-P4** and on the desktop. One encoder, so **RTSP and [HLS](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/light/drivers.html#hls) run one at a time**. See [the details below](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/light/drivers.html#rtsp-details).

read-only: `url` to play. The card's status line names the connected viewer.

guide.title: RTSP, details
guide.text: **Playing the stream.** Any RTSP player opens the `url` the card shows. These two are what the driver is tested against: `-fflags nobuffer -flags low_delay` is what makes ffplay show the stream as it arrives rather than filling a buffer first, which is the whole point of reaching for RTSP. VLC buffers about a second by default, so `--network-caching=100` brings it closer. **Watching LEDs on a monitor.** A grid is small in pixels and large in meaning, so scale it up with nearest-neighbor and each light stays a crisp square instead of a blurred blob: `-probesize 32 -analyzeduration 0` skips the startup probing, so the picture appears at once. `format=yuv420p` silences ffplay's `No accelerated colorspace conversion` notice, which reports a missing SIMD path in the player's own window conversion and says nothing about the stream. **The newest viewer is the viewer.** One session plays at a time, since each viewer costs another send on a device that is also driving lights. A new connection takes the session over rather than being refused. The reason is that a player which vanishes without `TEARDOWN` leaves a socket open and silent, and TCP reports a peer's absence only to a write it stops acknowledging, so waiting on that would strand the stream for minutes. The displaced viewer sees its connection close, which every player reports. **UDP carries the video.** The control conversation runs over TCP on port 554, and the frames go to the UDP port the viewer names in `SETUP`. A network that blocks that port pair leaves the stream silent while the session looks connected. A player asking for interleaved TCP instead is told so by code, since this server speaks UDP. **The rate is what the device renders.** `targetFps` is a ceiling rather than a promise: a heavy effect that ticks at 8 fps is streamed at 8 fps, since a frame that was never rendered cannot be sent. A stream slower than expected is therefore a question about the render loop rather than the transport. Each module's own tick time in the UI says which effect is spending the time. **The delay that remains is the codec's.** H.264 emits a frame once it has the whole frame, and a decoder holds one more, so tens of milliseconds stay whatever the transport does. What RTSP removes is HLS's segment buffering, which is the seconds.

targetFps.line: Encode-rate ceiling, which is also the keyframe interval.

scale.line: Video pixels per light (0 = auto). Each light is a solid block, never a blur.

PanelCardDriver.line: Streams the buffer to **ColorLight 5A-75 receiving cards** as raw Ethernet, taking the place of the sending card that normally feeds them.
PanelCardDriver.summary:
The board renders and sends, so it replaces a host PC driving the same wall. The link requirement and the protocol lineage are in [the details below](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/light/drivers.html#panel-card-details).

**No geometry controls**: the wall comes from the [Layout](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/moonmodules/light/layouts.html), cut into card rows.

guide.title: Panel Card, details
guide.text: **These cards need a 1 Gbit link**, not for bandwidth but for wire time. A 256x256 panel at 40 fps is only about 65 Mbit/s, but the cards have no buffering and latch on the sync frame, so a whole frame must arrive inside the inter-frame window. At 100 Mbit the same bytes take ten times as long, which breaks that timing and shows as tearing or wrong rows rather than as an error. The driver reads the negotiated speed and warns, but still sends: a small panel may be fine, and a measurement beats a refusal. **No IP is involved**, no address, no port, no DHCP, so the driver works on a link that never got a lease. A row wider than 497 pixels goes out as several packets. **The `interface` dropdown lists DETECTED adapters**, friendly names on Windows via Npcap and kernel names on Linux and macOS, re-listed on every control change so a hot-plugged NIC appears. The choice is remembered by adapter name rather than by index, so it survives reboots and Npcap reinstalls. `none (capture only)` records frames without sending. Raw sending is privileged: root or `CAP_NET_RAW` on Linux, BPF access on macOS, [Npcap](https://npcap.com/) or WinPcap on Windows; without it the driver records frames instead and says so. Step by step per OS: [Driving LED panels with a receiving card](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/how-to/panel-cards.html). **Card firmware.** v13 and newer act on the *second* copy of the brightness and sync frames, so both are sent twice; v12 and older act on the first and take a second sync as another latch. Reading and changing a card's version: [the tutorial](https://moonmodules.org/MoonLight/how-to/panel-cards.html#7-card-firmware-and-the-flicker). Protocol references: [FPP's ColorLight-5a-75.cpp](https://github.com/FalconChristmas/fpp/blob/master/src/channeloutput/ColorLight-5a-75.cpp) is the implementation this driver's byte layout agrees with. Harald Kubota's [5A-75B protocol write-up](https://hkubota.wordpress.com/2022/01/31/winter-project-colorlight-5a-75b-protocol/) documents the same wire format independently, including the brightness and color-temperature bytes and the discovery exchange. Read the write-up with its comments: a reader supplied the controller-number field that makes multiple cards on one segment distinguishable. The article's own MAC pair is printed the other way round from FPP's (destination `11:22:33:44:55:66`, source `22:22:33:44:55:66`, which is what this driver sends and what the cards filter on). Its lineage runs back to the [original mplayer-colorlight reverse engineering](http://www.mylifesucks.de/oss/mplayer-colorlight/).

firmware.line: `v12 and older` or `v13 and newer`. Wrong, and the wall barely updates.

interface.line: Which NIC to send from, by adapter name. Desktop only; raw sending needs privileges.

Hub75Driver.line: Drives **HUB75 LED panels straight from the board's GPIO**, with no receiving card in between.
Hub75Driver.summary:
